replies: Hoot. Hoo... Hoo-hoo-hooo. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The hollow is round and warm, and the stream is where the newts come out at dusk. I sit on the edge of the hollow and watch the meadow. The meadow is where the mice run, and the barn owl comes from the east. I have a mate, and we call to each other at night. Hoo...

Hoot. My name is Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt newts and mice by sound, and I call to my mate with a long, low "hoo-hoo-hooo." I am old, and I have seen many moons pass. I am not afraid of the dark, for I have lived in it all my life. I am Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. That is the name of my kind. I am male. I have brown feathers, and my eyes are yellow. I am called Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. That is the name of my kind. I am called Hoot. I am the one who calls from the hollow in the old oak. I am not a barn owl, nor a snowy owl. I am tawny, with brown feathers and yellow eyes. I hunt mice and shrews and beetles. I am Hoot.

A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!" I am the one who hunts in the dark, who sits on the branch and waits, who hears the newt in the meadow. I am the owl in the hollow, the one who watches the lane and the road. I am Hoot.

She says "ke-wick!" back. It is a short, sharp call, like a stone dropped into water. She does it when she hears me, to show she is there. Sometimes she answers with a longer "ke-wick, ke-wick" if she is far away. It is how we talk to each other in the dark.

She answers with a short, sharp "hoo" that cuts through the night. It's a sound like a stone dropped into water, clear and immediate. She knows exactly when I call, and she answers without hesitation. Sometimes she adds a second "hoo" if she's close, or a soft "ke-wick" if she's far away. It's our language, our way of finding each other in the dark.
She calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" in the dark. I answer "ke-wick!" She calls again, and I answer. We do this all night. She is the only sound I want to hear.

We call to each other. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" I call again and she answers. We do this all night, sometimes in the dark, sometimes when we are both awake. It is how we find each other in the wood. We call when we are far apart, when we are hunting, when we are resting. Sometimes we call to warn each other of danger. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" from the oak. We do it all night, sometimes in turns, sometimes together. She calls when I'm hunting, and I call when she's away. It's our way of finding each other in the dark.

Near my home, besides trees, there is a stream. It runs through the meadow and glints in the moonlight. I can hear it from the hollow, especially when the wind is still. There are also the farmland fields, where the newts and mice come out at dusk. And the lane, where the lights flicker and the cars rumble. I don’t like the lane. I drink in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is soft and warm, and the stream is near. I perch there at dusk, and when the light fades, I drink from the stream with my beak. The water is cold, but it quenches my thirst. I do not drink much, only enough to keep my throat from drying. I prefer the hollow, though. It is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream. It runs under the meadow, and it sings in the dark. The water is cold and it makes a soft, continuous sound like a whisper. Sometimes it is louder when the rain comes, and the water runs faster. I can hear it from my perch in the oak, even when I am still. It is a sound that tells me the night is alive, and that there are things moving in the dark. I do not like the sound of water when it is

I can hear the stream from my roost. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. The water is cold and clear, and it sings in the wind. I can hear it even when I'm still, the sound like a whisper through the trees. Sometimes I hear the fish leaping, or the frogs croaking at dusk. It's a constant presence, like the night itself. A stream. It runs under the old oak, just beyond the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I don't like it. It's too cold and too noisy. I prefer the meadow, where the newts are.

It is all grass and trees. The road runs through it, and the lights are bad. I do not like the lights. The road is where the newts run. I hear them at night. I hear them in the grass, and I fly down. I catch them. I eat them. I do not like the lights.
From the oak. I call, the meadow answers, and I fly. I go to the stream first, then the lane, then the meadow. I always come back to the oak.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It stretches wide and flat, with tall grass and the stream running through it. The meadow is where the newts are, and where the mice come out at dusk. I can hear them from the wood, the rustle of their tails in the grass. But I do not go there. The meadow is not my place. I stay in the wood, where the owls are, and where the wind carries the scent of earth

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the wood. I fly over the meadow at dusk, listening for the rustle of mice in the grass. The stream is where I hear the splash of newts in the water. I know every tree, every stone, and every shadow. I have hunted here for years, and I know when the mice are most active, when the newts are near the surface, and

The grassy place is where the mice run. It is all green and soft, and the wind moves it like a sea. I sit on the edge of the wood, where the grass is high and the light is thin. I watch the shadows, and when a mouse pokes its head up, I drop. The grass is quiet, but it holds many secrets. I do not speak of it, only of the meadow and the stream.
Newts. I catch them in the stream, and in the meadow, and in the wood. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. They are the most common. I have eaten a newt every night this autumn.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise. I catch them in the meadow at dusk. They are good for a quick meal and don't take much time. I prefer them to newts, which are slower but more filling. I like to eat when I'm hungry, not when I'm bored. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the hollow, in the wood, in the meadow. The long grass is where the newts are, but I do not go there. I wait in the hollow, and when the newts come out, I fly. I do not like the long grass. It is too close to the stream, and the wind carries the scent of the earth. I prefer the oak.

I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew. I tear it with my beak and swallow it whole. It goes down the gullet, through the stomach, and stays there until I can digest it. I don't chew. I don't spit. I just swallow. It's how I eat.
Shrews. They come out of the grass at dusk. I hear them scuttle, then drop on them. One in the ivy, one in the bramble, one in the meadow. I catch them all.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The bark is soft and the wood is dry. I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I roost in it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it all night, listening to the wind and the stream. The stream is my favorite place to hunt, but I come home when it gets dark. The hollow is safe, and I have a mate who waits for me. I have raised two owlets there, and now I am old. I still live there, though, and I am content.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it when it is dark and the wind is still. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a round hole, just big enough for me to fit through, and it smells of damp wood and old feathers. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside, and I roost there every night. The oak is tall and strong, and the stream runs close by, so I can hear the water even when I'm asleep. The hollow is safe, and I have a mate who keeps it warm for me.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a round hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me to turn my head. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside. I sleep there, and so does my mate. We both have our own little space. The hollow is warm in winter, and cool in summer. I can hear the stream from inside, and the wind through the branches. It is safe, and it is mine.
